title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) that measured whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—shared initial LLM candidate (declared: gpt-5-mini) + a deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. Planned N=300 pairs; 266 complete pairs were analysed after preregistered exclusion of 34 both‑arm provider failures. Observed contingency: n11=260, n10=5, n01=0, n00=1 (baseline success = 260/266 = 0.97744; guarded final success = 265/266 = 0.99624). Paired difference = 0.01879699248. The preregistered primary hypothesis test was the exact two‑sided McNemar test (α=0.05); it did not reject (p = 0.0625). We also report a paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601] as a supplementary descriptive interval. Repairs were invoked 6 times; median repair iterations per analysed pair = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and thus the preregistered latency estimand could not be evaluated. All execution and analysis artifacts (provider traces, validator traces, reconciliation manifest) are archived to support reproducibility.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models are being actively applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→CLI translation, zero‑touch configuration synthesis, and automated maintenance workflows [1], but stochastic generation can produce syntactic errors, incorrect command ordering, or topology‑dependent semantic violations that pose operational risk. A pragmatic mitigation pattern interposes a deterministic verifier (e.g., Batfish‑style reachability and policy checks) and a bounded repair loop around an LLM generator; we use the shorthand generate–verify–repair (GVR) for that architecture [3,4]. Prior literature presents prototypes and method proposals for GVR in code and domain‑specific generation, and NetOps work recommends grounding and verifier integration, yet preregistered, paired evaluations that archive verifier traces and precisely quantify verifier‑triggered repair benefits on reproducible task banks remain limited [1,2,3,4,5].

We tested the preregistered research question recorded in manifest cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1: under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one sampled initial LLM candidate per task used for both arms), does a GVR pipeline that permits at most one validator‑triggered automated repair call increase the proportion of tasks that pass a deterministic verifier compared to the same initial candidate evaluated without repair? Our contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation that reports exact paired contingency counts, the preregistered exact McNemar decision result, supplementary bootstrap intervals, execution accounting (model calls and repair counts), representative repaired episodes, and a focused limitations discussion grounded in the archived artifacts.
sections.related_work: LLM‑for‑NetOps research includes intent→configuration benchmarks (e.g., NetConfEval) and surveys documenting common failure modes—hallucination, constraint violations, and brittle prompt sensitivity—that motivate grounding and verification strategies [1,2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures have been proposed in adjacent problem domains to obtain deterministic acceptance for stochastic generators [3]. Network verification tools (Batfish, header‑space analyses) provide automatable checks appropriate as verifier oracles, though their rule coverage and scalability produce tradeoffs that constrain effectiveness as a universal oracle [4]. Empirical studies on what LLMs need to synthesize correct router/device configs emphasize explicit sequencing, vendor‑dialect handling, and constraint encoding as key factors; these findings motivate verifier‑driven repair when first‑pass generation omits required structure [5]. Our study differs by executing a preregistered paired test under shared_initial_candidate semantics and archiving per‑episode validator traces for auditability.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We followed the preregistration cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each task a single sampled initial model candidate is produced and used to compute (a) baseline outcome = validator(initial_candidate) and (b) guarded outcome = validator(initial_candidate) unless the validator fails, in which case at most one LLM repair call is permitted and its repaired output is re‑scored by the same deterministic validator. This design isolates the incremental effect of a validator‑triggered, bounded repair on the same initial draw and matches the preregistered execution_contract (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate").

Primary inferential procedure (preregistered): The preregistered, primary hypothesis test and decision rule was the exact two‑sided McNemar test at α=0.05 (estimator id: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). We record that explicitly here: the McNemar test is the preregistered decision procedure and governs the confirmatory claim. The paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) reported in Results is presented as a supplementary/descriptive interval estimator and was not the preregistered primary decision rule; we report it to convey effect magnitude and resampling uncertainty but we do not use it to overturn the preregistered McNemar decision. These procedures and bootstrap parameters are archived in the analysis artifacts (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Task bank, sampling, and exclusions: The preregistered task bank generation produced 300 intent→CLI pairs stratified into two vendor clusters (150 Cisco‑like, 150 Juniper‑like) from a deterministic generator with archived seeds; the task manifest and representative tasks are included in the evidence bundle. Provider/API transient failures were handled per the preregistered missingness rules: up to two automatic retries per failed model call; pairs where both arms failed due to infrastructure/model API errors were excluded from the primary confirmatory analysis under the 'complete_pair_primary' rule. In this run 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded and 266 complete pairs were analysed; this application of the preregistered missingness rule is recorded in the deterministic reconciliation artifact (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, sha256 = 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490).

Model configuration and stage semantics (provider/stage accounting clarification): The declared model recorded in execution/model_configuration.json is gpt-5-mini. The run recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 6}. To avoid confusion: under shared_initial_candidate semantics the stage label 'shared_initial_generation' denotes the single sampled candidate produced per task and reused to evaluate both baseline and guarded outcomes; the 'repair' stage count denotes additional model calls invoked only when that shared initial candidate failed the deterministic validator. The provider 'condition_counts' and stage tallies are model‑call accounting (how many model calls executed in each pipeline stage), not independent per‑arm full generation tallies. These semantics are reflected and reconciled in the archived provider_call_audit and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution summary and accounting: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms). Completed episodes = 532; failed episodes = 68. Applying the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' exclusion yielded complete_pairs = 266. Provider accounting: model_calls_used = 306 and repair_calls = 6 (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 6). All per‑episode raw responses, validator traces, and scoring JSONs are archived and hashed in the evidence bundle.

Primary paired outcomes and inferential summary: For the 266 analysed pairs the verifier contingency was n11 = 260 (both baseline and guarded pass), n10 = 5 (guarded-only pass), n01 = 0 (baseline-only pass), n00 = 1 (both fail). Observed per‑condition success rates: baseline = 260/266 = 0.9774436090; guarded = 265/266 = 0.9962406015; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.01879699248. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant counts (n10 = 5, n01 = 0) produced p = 0.0625, which does not meet the preregistered α = 0.05 decision rule. The paired bootstrap percentile CI (B = 10,000, seed = 1729) is [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601] and is reported as supplementary descriptive evidence. The discrepancy between the exact discrete McNemar p‑value and the bootstrap CI is a finite‑sample artefact when discordant counts are small; both summaries are reported so readers can weigh formal hypothesis rejection against effect magnitude and CI width.

Repair yield and derived operational scalars: Repairs were invoked 6 times; among analysed pairs at most five repair invocations appear to have converted a baseline fail into a guarded pass (consistent with n10 = 5). Median repair iterations per analysed pair = 0 (most pairs required no repair). A descriptive number‑needed‑to‑treat (NNT) analog = 1 / absolute_risk_reduction ≈ 53.2 (1/0.01879699248), indicating roughly 53 guarded tasks were associated with one additional verifier‑approved configuration under these run conditions; interpret this scalar cautiously because the baseline pass rate was high, producing limited repair opportunities.

Representative repaired episode diagnostics: Representative per‑episode validator traces illustrate typical failure and repair behavior and are archived (e.g., task-000008: the shared initial candidate exhibited a truncated final token causing parsed_command_count < required_command_count and failed the validator; the automated repair produced a completed command sequence and the guarded final trace shows validation_after.valid = true). Per‑episode artifacts include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation codes, and repair_prompt traces to enable targeted auditing of repair logic and verifier coverage.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation: The observed absolute improvement is small and the preregistered McNemar test did not reject at α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI excluding zero highlights finite‑sample uncertainty and a positive point estimate, but the McNemar decision rule was the preregistered confirmatory gate and therefore controls our formal confirmatory claim. With few discordant pairs (n10 + n01 = 5) the exact McNemar two‑sided test is conservative; the bootstrap CI is informative about magnitude but is labeled and used here only as descriptive supplementary evidence.

Operational implications and boundary conditions: The corpus had a high baseline first‑pass success (≈97.7%), so repair opportunities were rare (6/300) and the marginal yield per repaired episode was small. In contexts with lower first‑pass accuracy, different sampling regimes (multiple initial draws), or broader validator failure coverage, GVR may yield larger absolute improvements. We did not evaluate interventions outside the preregistered estimand (e.g., independent multiple initial draws or constrained first‑pass prompting) because those arms were not preregistered nor executed; doing so would require independent initial generations per arm and a different estimand.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolates validator‑triggered repair effect for a fixed sampled draw but does not measure effects of other generator‑level interventions. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies a finite, archived rule battery (syntactic parsing, required_sequence, constrained_field checks, reachability); semantic violations outside that battery are unmeasured. External validity: tasks derive from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor dialect clusters; results may not generalize to other vendors, larger topologies, or production heterogeneity. Conclusion validity: 34 both‑arm provider failures reduced effective N and limited power for small effect detection.

Design recommendations (artifact‑grounded): (1) when baseline pass rates are high, increase power by targeting lower‑baseline corpora or adding arms with multiple independent initial draws or constrained prompting; (2) archive per‑episode timing to assess latency against operational bounds—the preregistered latency estimand could not be evaluated because timing was not archived; (3) publish and expand validator rule coverage and include tests for verifier false negatives; per‑episode validator traces included in the evidence bundle enable such audits.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired evaluation (shared_initial_candidate semantics) of a GVR pipeline (declared model: gpt‑5‑mini; deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5), we observed a small absolute guarded increase in deterministic‑verifier pass rate (0.01879699248) across 266 analysed pairs, but the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reject at α=0.05 (p=0.0625). A paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) is reported as supplementary descriptive evidence. Repairs were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per analysed task = 0. The experiment, artifacts, and reconciliations (including provider accounting and per‑episode validator traces) are archived to support reanalysis and further study of GVR boundary conditions and alternative generation semantics.

Execution and analysis artifacts, provider traces, and validator traces are archived in the evidence bundle referenced in the preregistration.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per preregistered rules (see analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, sha256 = 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490), reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.

Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic sampling seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
H2 latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
